In 2024, 12.8% of Alberta children under 18 were living in poverty. That uses the Market Basket Measure (2023 base), which is Canada's official poverty line. It is up from 11.9% in 2023.

On the Low Income Measure after tax (LIM-AT), the 2024 rate was 13.9%, up from 13.5% in 2023.

Both come from the Canadian Income Survey. 2024 is the latest year available.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 11-10-0135-01. The vectors are v1792632015 for the MBM and v96520326 for the LIM-AT.

Alberta's provincial and territorial public administration paid an average of **$1,702.65 per week in 2025**. That is for all employees, including overtime, and it comes from the annual series. It works out to roughly $88,500 a year if you multiply by 52, but that is my arithmetic and StatCan doesn't publish it.

- **Recent annual figures:** 2023 was $1,703.25 and 2024 was $1,677.47.
- **Latest month:** August 2026 was $1,883.03 per week. June and July 2026 were $1,877.87 and $1,877.58. These monthly figures are not seasonally adjusted.
- **Hourly wage:** I did not pull an hourly wage rate for this industry. These figures are weekly earnings.

Source: Statistics Canada, Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH). The annual figure is from table 14-10-0204-01 (vector v1742415) and the monthly figures from table 14-10-0203-01 (vector v1560358).

In 2024, the average total income of individuals in Alberta was **$63,200**. That is down from $63,900 in 2023. It is the average for all persons, both sexes, in current dollars. Total income here is income before tax.

I didn't pull the after-tax or median figures, which are in the same table.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 11-10-0091-01 (Canadian Income Survey), vector v1529672282, reference period 2024.

I couldn't find a poverty rate for people with disabilities in Alberta. Statistics Canada doesn't publish one in the table I checked.

Table 11-10-0090-01, "Poverty and low-income statistics by disability status", covers Canada only. It has no provincial breakdown, and I found no other table that gives one.

The national figure is the closest available. In 2024, 12.6% of Canadians aged 15 and over with disabilities were in poverty, measured by the Market Basket Measure (2023 base). That is vector v1793292452, and its data quality rating is "very good". Other measures, including the after-tax Low Income Measure, are in the same table.

In August 2026 Quebec's rate was higher, at 60.6% against Ontario's 60.2%.

The unadjusted figures for August 2026 are slightly higher, at 2.9% and 529,415 vacancies.

**Prince Edward Island** had the highest 12-month CPI inflation in September 2026, at about **5.7%**. Nova Scotia was next at 5.6%, then New Brunswick at 5.0%.

I worked this out from the All-items index (2002=100) rather than reading a published rate. The index was 177.6 in September 2026 and 168.1 in September 2025. That is 5.7% after rounding. Because I rounded from index levels, StatCan's own published rate could differ by 0.1 point.

The territories' cities (Whitehorse, Yellowknife, Iqaluit) were left out of the comparison, since they aren't provinces.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0004-01 (CPI, monthly, not seasonally adjusted), All-items, PEI vector v41691379, reference period September 2026 against September 2025.

Canada's real GDP grew about **3.3% at an annualized rate** in Q2 2026. That is my calculation from the published levels, not a figure StatCan lists directly. StatCan's own quarter-over-quarter change is **0.8%**.

- Q1 2026 was $2,503,604 million, in chained 2017 dollars, seasonally adjusted at annual rates.
- Q2 2026 was $2,524,127 million on the same basis.
- The quarterly change is 2,524,127 / 2,503,604 − 1 = 0.82%.
- Annualizing that gives (1.0082)^4 − 1 ≈ 3.3%.

The table's "percentage change" series shows 0.8% for Q2. That is the quarterly rate, not an annualized one. I didn't find an annualized headline rate for total GDP in this table, and the 3.3% is rounded from the unrounded levels.

Source: Statistics Canada, table 36-10-0104-01, GDP at market prices, Canada, Q2 2026 (released 2026-08-28). Vector v62305752 holds the levels and v1594571783 holds the quarterly percentage change.

Building permits issued in Canada in August 2026 were worth about **$13.0 billion** unadjusted, in current dollars. The figure is $12,997,151 thousand.

The seasonally adjusted value was about $13.43 billion ($13,429,718 thousand). Both figures cover all residential and non-residential permits and all types of work. They come from the table's current release, dated 2026-11-12. That release also includes September 2026 data.
